title: Dhanna the farmer
hook: Dhanna prays plainly for flour, lentils, ghee, a cow and a good wife (Dhanasri, Dhanna, ang 695)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Beni: the photos of a life, forgetting in every one. Your line was remember at every stage. Did your chosen moment come, and did you stop? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

O Gopal, I'm a beggar at Your door. That's how one hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib begins, in paraphrase, and what follows sounds less like poetry than a shopping list. Between hymns about the soul and the Infinite, there it sits. It belongs to Dhanna, a farmer, and it's addressed straight to God. He doesn't dress it up or explain himself. He stands at the door and asks for groceries.
screen: `O GOPAL, A BEGGAR AT YOUR DOOR.` → `BETWEEN HYMNS OF THE SOUL, A LIST.` → `DHANNA ASKS FOR GROCERIES.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 695. It opens with the word aarta. Some read it as one in need, a beggar at the door; others hear in it aarti, an offering of worship. In paraphrase: O Gopal, Sustainer of the world, I'm a beggar at Your door; You take care of the work of those who are devoted to You. Then comes the list. Lentils, flour and ghee, so my heart can be content each day. Shoes, and good clothes. Grain. A cow and a buffalo that give milk. A fine horse. And a good wife to keep the home. The last line: your servant Dhanna asks for these. That's it. No apology, no explanation that what he really wants is something higher. Notice what kind of things they are. Food for the table. Something on the feet. Animals that keep a farm alive. A partner. It's the list of a working household, said out loud to the Lord as if the Lord were the one who could be asked. And the hymn stands in the Guru's book, beside songs of longing for the Lord. Why does that matter? Because some people feel a prayer has to be cleaned up before it's said: made noble, made about other people, the part about rent hidden. Dhanna's hymn sits there quietly saying the plain thing is allowed. Trust shows up in the asking. Tradition tells other stories about Dhanna, about a stone and a simple farmer's faith, and we'll leave those for another day. Today it's just the list, and the man who wasn't embarrassed to say it to God.
screen: `A BEGGAR AT YOUR DOOR, GOPAL.` · `LENTILS, FLOUR, GHEE, SHOES, A COW.` · `KEPT IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · then, large: `THE PLAIN THING IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for a plain thing, if you pray. If you don't, simply name one. Use the sit to find it: not the noblest need you have, the most ordinary one. Groceries for the week. A night of sleep. A car that starts. A kind word at work. Say it plainly, without decorating it. If you pray, offer it as Dhanna did, as someone asking at a door. If you don't, hold it honestly as a need. You can also say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Dhanna the farmer. The Bhagat of Raag Dhanasri who asked the Lord for lentils, flour, ghee, shoes, a cow and a good wife, and whose list sits in the Guru's book.
Your line: plain prayers count. Today, when a small need shows up, don't wave it away; name it plainly, once. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Dhanna's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bring ordinary needs as well as spiritual ones into ardas, the standing prayer.

fork.setup: you're Dhanna, a farmer, standing before the Lord with real needs at home. what do you say?
options: name the groceries, the cow and the shoes, plainly.
say nothing, so as not to bother God.
fork.reveal: he names them all, plainly, as a beggar at the door, and the hymn sits in the Guru's book.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the hymn's opening (Ang 695). aarta is read by some as 'one in need at Your door', by others as 'Your aarti'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy book would only hold lofty prayers.
what it means: a farmer's grocery list, said to God, kept in the Guru's book.
what a scholar hears: the list maps a working farm household, food, clothes, animals, a partner, all brought to the door of Gopal.

notes: Hymn paraphrased from memory (gopal tera aarta; daal seedha maagau gheeo; panheea chhaadan neeka; anaaj magau sat seeka; gaoo bhais magau laaveree; ik taajan turee changeree; ghar kee geehan changee). Confirm the list. 'Sat seeka' (sevenfold grain) is rendered simply as 'grain' to avoid an unchecked count.
'aarta' is glossed as 'a beggar at Your door'; some read it as a humble supplicant or one in need. Please check.
The stone story of Dhanna is mentioned only as 'tradition tells other stories'; confirm.
The 'cleaned up' line is the writer's framing; editor may cut.

Editor: replaced the fridge-list hook (another object-list opener) with the hymn's opening line; cut the unsourced claim that the Gurus didn't edit the hymn (screen, fork, trapdoor too) and the superlative 'deepest longing'; trimmed the doubled 'if you pray' in the practice.

Audit: hook screen still showed the cut fridge-list image (`A LIST ON THE FRIDGE.`); replaced to match the voice. The original note claimed aarta is 'usually' read as beggar; widely used translations also render it 'this is Your aarti', so both readings are now named.
